summary: Simon Willison describes shipping a Newsletters page on his blog by talking to the Codex tab of the ChatGPT desktop app in voice mode for about half an hour while cooking dinner. The model (GPT-6 Astra High) built the Django model, migration, four import functions, archive pages and search integration. He then opened a PR, reviewed it, and spent another half hour typing to fix an import and tweak the display. He concludes voice plus a visual preview is useful for multi-tasking but he would not use it as a daily driver, because typing and pasting are more efficient for details.
relevance_reason: A first-hand, practitioner account of using a voice-driven coding agent on a real task. It covers the brief's voice/conversational question (voice vs typing vs screens) and also touches on agents operating a dev environment, and it separates what worked from where voice falls short.
themes: Voice as a front end for coding agents
Voice vs typing and direct manipulation

claims.claim: Willison built the Newsletters feature almost entirely by voice using the Codex tab of the ChatGPT desktop app in voice conversation mode, against a local dev environment.
claims.quote: I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner.

claims.claim: The voice session, with its disfluent, rambling transcript, was clear enough for the model to understand the requirements, and the half-hour conversation produced a model, migration, four imports, archive pages and search integration.
claims.quote: Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build!

claims.claim: The voice session did not fully finish the job: the import design needed a keyboard session, and after review he spent another half hour of typed prompting fixing an import mechanism and tweaking display before deploying.
claims.quote: It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR.

claims.claim: The visual preview and the option to type or paste make this a more powerful way to use a coding agent than phone-only voice mode.
claims.quote: The addition of the visual preview, plus being able to type or paste things in via the keyboard when I need to communicate something that doesn't work vocally

claims.claim: For detailed work, typing, pasting examples and error messages, or highlighting code is more efficient than describing changes in words, so voice won't be his daily driver.
claims.quote: Being able to paste in examples and error messages, or directly highlight the code or feature that needs changing, remains more efficient than trying to describe it in words.

claims.claim: The main benefit of voice is multi-tasking, such as building things while cooking, and he would not use it in a shared workspace.
claims.quote: The killer feature for me is the ability to multi-task. I usually cook with a podcast or TikTok running; now I can actually build stuff instead.

claims.claim: Voice-driven demos like this are a favourite of OpenAI's at events such as DevDay, and they work well there.
claims.quote: OpenAI love using voice-driven demos like this one for things like DevDay - and they do work well in that environment.

commercial_interest: No sponsorship disclosed for this post. Willison is an independent blogger who runs a Substack and a sponsors-only newsletter, which are the subject of the feature built. He writes about OpenAI tools as a user, with no stated vendor relationship.
older_event: No. The item reports a new hands-on use (published 2026-10-09) rather than an older event. The model and voice mode are described as current tools, and the build itself was shipped that day.
